meta.title: US edition theory quiz (Accounting 101 level, original)

questions.stem: The company has total assets of $80,000 and total liabilities of $30,000. What is total equity?
questions.explanation: Equity is assets minus liabilities, so $80,000 - $30,000 = $50,000. This comes straight from the accounting equation.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. If you know two parts, you can find the third by subtraction.

wrongReasons.1: Adding assets and liabilities does not follow the equation.
wrongReasons.2: $30,000 is the liabilities, not the equity.
wrongReasons.3: $80,000 is total assets, which equals liabilities plus equity.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a liability?
options: Something the company owns that has value
An obligation to pay or provide something to another party
The owners' claim on the assets
A cost used up to earn revenue
questions.answerText: An obligation to pay or provide something to another party
questions.explanation: A liability is something the company owes, such as accounts payable or a loan. It is a claim by outsiders on the company's assets.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Liabilities are present obligations that come from past events. They will be settled with cash, goods, or services.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A liability is an obligation owed to someone outside the business.

wrongReasons.1: That describes an asset.
wrongReasons.3: That describes equity.
wrongReasons.4: That describes an expense.

questions.stem: Which account normally has a credit balance?
options: Dividends
Supplies
Rent Expense
Common Stock
questions.answerText: Common Stock
questions.explanation: Common Stock is an equity account, and equity increases with credits. Dividends, supplies, and expenses all increase with debits.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Assets, expenses, and dividends normally have debit balances. Liabilities, equity, and revenue normally have credit balances.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Common Stock is equity, so its normal balance is a credit.

wrongReasons.1: Dividends is a contra equity account with a normal debit balance.
wrongReasons.2: Supplies is an asset, so it normally has a debit balance.
wrongReasons.3: Expenses increase with debits, so Rent Expense has a debit balance.

questions.stem: Which event is recorded as an accounting transaction?
options: A customer says it will place a large order next month
The company signed a letter promising to hire an employee
The owner predicts that sales will rise
Paid $900 cash for 12 months of insurance
questions.answerText: Paid $900 cash for 12 months of insurance
questions.explanation: A transaction changes assets, liabilities, or equity and can be measured. Paying for insurance does that; promises and predictions do not.

deepDive.conceptExplain: An event is recorded only if it changes the accounting equation and has a reliable dollar amount.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Paying cash for insurance reduces Cash and creates Prepaid Insurance.

wrongReasons.1: A future order does not change any account yet.
wrongReasons.2: A promise to hire is not yet an exchange of value.
wrongReasons.3: A prediction is not a completed event.

questions.stem: The company bought equipment for $5,000 cash. What happens to total assets?
options: They increase by $5,000
They stay the same
They decrease by $5,000
They increase by $10,000
questions.answerText: They stay the same
questions.explanation: Equipment goes up by $5,000 and Cash goes down by $5,000. One asset replaces another, so the total is unchanged.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Some transactions only swap one asset for another. Then both sides of the equation stay the same.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Equipment +$5,000 and Cash -$5,000 net to zero.

wrongReasons.1: Cash decreased by the same amount, so the total did not rise.
wrongReasons.3: Total assets did not fall because equipment was received.
wrongReasons.4: Nothing doubles the amount.

questions.stem: Purchased supplies on account for $400. How is the accounting equation affected?
options: Assets +$400 and equity +$400
Assets +$400 and liabilities +$400
Assets +$400 and assets -$400
Liabilities +$400 and equity -$400
questions.answerText: Assets +$400 and liabilities +$400
questions.explanation: Supplies is an asset that increases. Because it was bought on account, Accounts Payable (a liability) also increases by $400.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Buying on credit adds an asset and a liability together. No cash moves until the bill is paid.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Dr Supplies 400 / Cr Accounts Payable 400.

wrongReasons.1: Equity does not change when you buy on account.
wrongReasons.3: Cash was not used, so no asset decreased.
wrongReasons.4: Nothing reduces equity in this purchase.

questions.stem: Performed a service and received $2,000 cash. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Service Revenue 2,000 / Cr Cash 2,000
Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Unearned Revenue 2,000
Dr Accounts Receivable 2,000 / Cr Cash 2,000
Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Service Revenue 2,000
questions.answerText: Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Service Revenue 2,000
questions.explanation: Cash increases, so Cash is debited. Service Revenue increases, so it is credited.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Revenue is earned when the service is done. Cash is debited and the revenue account is credited.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Cash is an asset that rises with a debit; revenue rises with a credit.

wrongReasons.1: That reverses the debit and credit.
wrongReasons.2: The service was already performed, so it is earned, not unearned.
wrongReasons.3: No receivable exists because cash was received.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a trial balance?
options: To show the company's net income for the year
To record transactions in date order
To check that total debits equal total credits
To prove that every entry was posted to the right account
questions.answerText: To check that total debits equal total credits
questions.explanation: A trial balance lists all ledger balances. If debits equal credits, the ledger is mathematically balanced.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The trial balance is a check, not a financial statement. It shows balance, but not that every entry is correct.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Equal totals show that debits and credits match.

wrongReasons.1: Net income is shown on the income statement.
wrongReasons.2: Recording in date order is the job of the journal.
wrongReasons.4: A trial balance can balance even with wrong-account errors.

questions.stem: Which error would NOT cause the trial balance to be out of balance?
options: Posting a debit twice
Leaving a credit out of the ledger
Debiting Supplies instead of Equipment for the right amount
Recording $63 as $36 in one account
questions.answerText: Debiting Supplies instead of Equipment for the right amount
questions.explanation: Wrong-account errors keep total debits equal to total credits. The other errors upset the totals.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A trial balance cannot find errors that keep debits equal to credits, such as the wrong account or an omitted entry.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Both sides stay equal, so the trial balance still balances.

wrongReasons.1: A duplicate debit makes debits too high.
wrongReasons.2: A missing credit makes credits too low.
wrongReasons.4: A transposition changes one side only.

questions.stem: A trial balance is out by an amount that is evenly divisible by 9. What does this often indicate?
options: A transposition error
An unrecorded transaction
Posting to the wrong account
A missing account
questions.answerText: A transposition error
questions.explanation: Swapping two digits, such as 63 to 36, changes the total by a multiple of 9. Look for this when the difference divides by 9.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A transposition switches adjacent digits. The resulting difference is always a multiple of 9.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Digit swaps create differences divisible by 9.

wrongReasons.2: An unrecorded transaction would not unbalance the trial balance.
wrongReasons.3: A wrong-account error keeps totals equal.
wrongReasons.4: A missing account would not give a multiple of 9.

questions.stem: Under the accrual basis, revenue is recognized when it is:
options: Earned
Billed to the customer
Collected in cash
Ordered by the customer
questions.answerText: Earned
questions.explanation: Accrual accounting records revenue when the company earns it, no matter when cash arrives.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Revenue is recorded when the performance obligation is met. Cash timing does not matter.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Earning the revenue triggers recognition.

wrongReasons.2: Billing does not always match when it is earned.
wrongReasons.3: That is the cash basis.
wrongReasons.4: An order is only a promise.

questions.stem: Which principle says expenses should be recorded in the same period as the revenues they helped earn?
options: Matching
Economic entity
Going concern
Cost
questions.answerText: Matching
questions.explanation: Matching links expenses to the revenue they produced. It is why adjusting entries are needed.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Costs used to earn a period's revenue are reported in that same period.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Matching puts expenses and related revenue together.

wrongReasons.2: Economic entity separates business and owners.
wrongReasons.3: Going concern assumes the business will keep operating.
wrongReasons.4: The cost principle records assets at what was paid.

questions.stem: Paid $1,200 for three months of rent in advance. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Rent Expense 1,200 / Cr Accounts Payable 1,200
Dr Prepaid Rent 1,200 / Cr Cash 1,200
Dr Cash 1,200 / Cr Prepaid Rent 1,200
Dr Rent Receivable 1,200 / Cr Cash 1,200
questions.answerText: Dr Prepaid Rent 1,200 / Cr Cash 1,200
questions.explanation: Rent paid in advance is an asset until used up. Cash decreases with a credit.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A prepayment gives future benefit, so it is first recorded as an asset.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Prepaid Rent is debited and Cash is credited.

wrongReasons.1: The company paid cash, not on account.
wrongReasons.3: That reverses the entry.
wrongReasons.4: The company is the tenant, so it has no rent receivable.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the first steps of the accounting cycle in the right order?
options: Post to the ledger, journalize, analyze transactions, prepare financial statements
Prepare financial statements, journalize, analyze transactions, close
Analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance
Journalize, close the books, analyze transactions, post
questions.answerText: Analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance
questions.explanation: You first analyze each event, then record it in the journal, post to ledger accounts, and test with a trial balance.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The cycle starts with analysis and ends with a post-closing trial balance.
deepDive.whyCorrect: That order follows the cycle.

wrongReasons.1: Posting cannot come before journalizing.
wrongReasons.2: Statements come after adjusting, not first.
wrongReasons.4: Closing is near the end of the cycle.

questions.stem: What does posting mean?
options: Recording an event in the journal for the first time
Transferring journal entry amounts to ledger accounts
Listing ledger balances to prove equality
Preparing the income statement
questions.answerText: Transferring journal entry amounts to ledger accounts
questions.explanation: Posting copies debits and credits from the journal into the ledger accounts. It gives each account an up-to-date balance.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Journalizing comes first. Posting then sorts the amounts by account.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Posting moves amounts from journal to ledger.

wrongReasons.1: That describes journalizing.
wrongReasons.3: That describes a trial balance.
wrongReasons.4: Statements are prepared from the ledger balances.

questions.stem: The Cash account has debits of $12,000 and credits of $7,500. What is the balance?
options: $4,500 credit
$19,500 debit
$4,500 debit
$7,500 debit
questions.answerText: $4,500 debit
questions.explanation: Subtract the smaller side from the larger: $12,000 - $7,500 = $4,500. Debits are larger, so it is a debit balance.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Balance = larger side minus smaller side. The larger side tells you the balance type.

wrongReasons.1: Debits are larger, so it is not a credit.
wrongReasons.2: You do not add debits and credits.
wrongReasons.4: $7,500 is just the credit total.

questions.stem: Revenues for the year were $25,000 and expenses were $18,400. What is net income?
questions.explanation: Net income is revenues minus expenses: $25,000 - $18,400 = $6,600.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Net income = Revenues - Expenses. A negative result is a net loss.

wrongReasons.1: Adding revenues and expenses is not net income.
wrongReasons.2: $18,400 is total expenses.
wrongReasons.4: $25,000 is revenue before subtracting expenses.

questions.stem: Beginning Retained Earnings were $40,000, net income was $12,000, and dividends were $5,000. What is ending Retained Earnings?
questions.explanation: Ending = beginning + net income - dividends: $40,000 + $12,000 - $5,000 = $47,000.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Retained Earnings grows with net income and shrinks with dividends.

wrongReasons.1: That adds the dividends instead of subtracting them.
wrongReasons.3: That ignores the dividends.
wrongReasons.4: That ignores the net income.

questions.stem: Which financial statement reports assets, liabilities, and equity at a single point in time?
options: Income statement
Balance sheet
Statement of retained earnings
Trial balance
questions.answerText: Balance sheet
questions.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot on a specific date. The income statement covers a period.

deepDive.conceptExplain: It follows the equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity at that date.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A balance sheet shows financial position on one date.

wrongReasons.1: The income statement covers a period of time.
wrongReasons.3: That statement explains changes in Retained Earnings.
wrongReasons.4: A trial balance is an internal check, not a statement.

questions.stem: Which account is reported on the income statement?
options: Dividends
Common Stock
Rent Expense
Unearned Revenue
questions.answerText: Rent Expense
questions.explanation: Revenues and expenses go on the income statement. Rent Expense is an expense.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Only revenue, expense, gain, and loss accounts appear on the income statement.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Rent Expense reduces net income.

wrongReasons.1: Dividends appear in the statement of retained earnings.
wrongReasons.2: Common Stock is on the balance sheet.
wrongReasons.4: Unearned Revenue is a liability on the balance sheet.

questions.stem: Which assumption requires the company's records to be kept separate from its owners' personal affairs?
options: Going concern assumption
Economic entity assumption
Monetary unit assumption
Time period assumption
questions.answerText: Economic entity assumption
questions.explanation: The business is treated as its own accounting unit. Owners' personal items stay out of its books.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Each business is a separate unit, even if it is owned by people with other interests.
deepDive.whyCorrect: That assumption separates the business from its owners.

wrongReasons.1: Going concern assumes the business will continue.
wrongReasons.3: Monetary unit says to record things in dollars.
wrongReasons.4: Time period divides life into reporting periods.

questions.stem: Provided services for $2,000: received $500 cash and the rest is due later. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Cash 500, Dr Accounts Receivable 1,500 / Cr Service Revenue 2,000
Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Service Revenue 2,000
Dr Cash 500 / Cr Service Revenue 500
Dr Accounts Receivable 2,000 / Cr Service Revenue 2,000
questions.answerText: Dr Cash 500, Dr Accounts Receivable 1,500 / Cr Service Revenue 2,000
questions.explanation: The company earned $2,000. It collected $500 and expects $1,500 more, so both Cash and Accounts Receivable are debited.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A compound entry has more than two accounts, but total debits still equal total credits.
deepDive.whyCorrect: 500 + 1,500 = 2,000 on the debit side, matching the credit.

wrongReasons.2: Only $500 cash was received.
wrongReasons.3: That records only part of the revenue.
wrongReasons.4: That ignores the cash collected.

questions.stem: Which item is reported as Cash on the balance sheet?
options: Funds in a checking account
A postdated check from a customer
Postage stamps on hand
An IOU from an employee
questions.answerText: Funds in a checking account
questions.explanation: Cash includes currency, checking balances, and money orders. The other items are not available to spend now.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Cash is anything the bank accepts at face value for deposit now.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A checking balance is available cash.

wrongReasons.2: A postdated check cannot be deposited yet.
wrongReasons.3: Stamps are supplies.
wrongReasons.4: An IOU is a receivable.

questions.stem: Which internal control principle is shown when the person who handles cash receipts does not keep the accounting records?
options: Prenumbered documents
Mandatory vacations
Establishing responsibility
Separation of duties
questions.answerText: Separation of duties
questions.explanation: Splitting custody from record keeping makes it harder to hide theft.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Different people should handle assets, record transactions, and approve them.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Cash handling and record keeping are split.

wrongReasons.1: That means forms are in number order.
wrongReasons.2: That means employees take time off.
wrongReasons.3: That means one person is accountable for each task.

questions.stem: Why does a company use prenumbered invoices and checks?
options: To speed up bank deposits
To account for every document and detect missing ones
To prevent customers from paying late
To reduce sales tax
questions.answerText: To account for every document and detect missing ones
questions.explanation: A missing number signals a lost or hidden document. This supports accountability.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Prenumbered forms must be accounted for in sequence.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Gaps in numbering point to problems.

wrongReasons.1: They do not speed deposits.
wrongReasons.3: They have no effect on customers' payment dates.
wrongReasons.4: They are unrelated to taxes.

questions.stem: Requiring employees to take vacations and rotating their duties is mostly meant to:
options: Increase sales
Help uncover fraud
Reduce payroll costs
Speed up closing
questions.answerText: Help uncover fraud
questions.explanation: Someone covering the job may notice hidden errors or theft.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Fraud is easier to hide when one person always does the same task.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A substitute may find irregularities.

wrongReasons.1: These steps are not for sales.
wrongReasons.3: They do not cut payroll costs.
wrongReasons.4: They do not affect closing time.

questions.stem: Only one cashier is assigned to each cash register drawer. Which control principle is this?
options: Separation of duties
Independent verification
Establishing responsibility
Physical controls
questions.answerText: Establishing responsibility
questions.explanation: If one person uses a drawer, any shortage can be traced to that person.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Each task should be assigned to one person, so accountability is clear.
deepDive.whyCorrect: One cashier per drawer sets clear responsibility.

wrongReasons.1: That is about splitting roles.
wrongReasons.2: That is checking work by someone else.
wrongReasons.4: That is locks, safes, or cameras.

questions.stem: Which statement about the limits of internal control is correct?
options: Collusion between employees can defeat controls
Good controls guarantee there will be no fraud
Controls are never worth the cost
Controls only work in large companies
questions.answerText: Collusion between employees can defeat controls
questions.explanation: When two employees work together, they can get around separation of duties.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Controls reduce risk but cannot eliminate it. People can collude or make mistakes.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Collusion can bypass controls.

wrongReasons.2: No system gives a guarantee.
wrongReasons.3: Many controls are cheap and useful.
wrongReasons.4: Small firms use controls too.

questions.stem: The bank balance is $8,200. Deposits in transit are $1,300 and outstanding checks are $900. What is the adjusted bank balance?
questions.explanation: Add deposits in transit and subtract outstanding checks: $8,200 + $1,300 - $900 = $8,600.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The bank side corrects for items the bank does not know about yet.

wrongReasons.1: That subtracts deposits and adds checks.
wrongReasons.3: That adds both items.
wrongReasons.4: That ignores the outstanding checks.

questions.stem: The book balance is $5,000. The bank collected a $600 note for the company, charged a $25 service fee, and returned a $150 NSF check. What is the adjusted book balance?

deepDive.conceptExplain: Items the bank has recorded but the company has not are adjusted on the book side.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Add the collection; subtract the fee and the NSF check.

wrongReasons.1: That adds the NSF check back.
wrongReasons.2: That does not subtract the fee.
wrongReasons.3: That subtracts the collection.

questions.stem: Which item on a bank reconciliation requires the company to make a journal entry?
options: Outstanding check
Deposit in transit
Bank service charge
A bank error in the company's favor
questions.answerText: Bank service charge
questions.explanation: Items the bank has recorded but the company has not are new to the company and need an entry. The bank has already recorded the service charge, but the company has not.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Timing items on the bank side need no entry. Items the company has not yet recorded do.
deepDive.whyCorrect: The service charge must be recorded: Dr Bank Service Charges / Cr Cash.

wrongReasons.1: It was already recorded in the books when the check was written.
wrongReasons.2: It was already recorded in the books when the deposit was made.
wrongReasons.4: The bank corrects its own error, so the company makes no entry.

questions.stem: Which reconciling item is subtracted from the bank balance?
options: Outstanding checks
Deposits in transit
NSF checks
Interest earned
questions.answerText: Outstanding checks
questions.explanation: Outstanding checks have been recorded in the books but have not yet cleared the bank.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Deposits in transit are added, and outstanding checks are subtracted.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Outstanding checks reduce the bank side.

wrongReasons.2: Those are added to the bank balance.
wrongReasons.3: Those are adjustments to the book side.
wrongReasons.4: Those are adjustments to the book side.

questions.stem: A customer's check from Harbor Goods is returned NSF. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Cash / Cr Accounts Receivable
Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Cash
Dr Sales Revenue / Cr Cash
Dr Accounts Receivable / Cr Cash
questions.answerText: Dr Accounts Receivable / Cr Cash
questions.explanation: The money did not arrive, so the company again has a receivable. The deposit is reversed with a credit to Cash.

deepDive.conceptExplain: An NSF check means the customer still owes the company.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Receivable is restored and Cash reduced.

wrongReasons.1: That reverses the entry.
wrongReasons.2: It is too early to call the debt uncollectible.
wrongReasons.3: Revenue is not reversed.

questions.stem: The company sets up a $200 petty cash fund by writing a check. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Cash 200 / Cr Petty Cash 200
Dr Office Expense 200 / Cr Cash 200
Dr Petty Cash 200 / Cr Cash 200
Dr Petty Cash 200 / Cr Office Expense 200
questions.answerText: Dr Petty Cash 200 / Cr Cash 200
questions.explanation: Cash moves from the bank account to the fund, both of which are assets.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A fund is created by moving cash into the Petty Cash account.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Petty Cash increases and Cash decreases.

wrongReasons.1: That reverses the entry.
wrongReasons.2: The expenses are recorded when the fund is replenished.
wrongReasons.4: That has no cash effect.

questions.stem: A $200 petty cash fund has receipts of $186 and $14 in cash. How much is the replenishment check?
questions.explanation: The check must bring cash back to $200: $200 - $14 = $186, equal to the receipts.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The check equals the amount spent.

wrongReasons.2: That is the cash still in the box.
wrongReasons.3: That would overfund the box.
wrongReasons.4: The fund is not full.

questions.stem: A $150 petty cash fund has $128 in receipts and $20 in cash. What is the replenishment check, and what does the difference mean?
options: $130; Cash Over and Short is debited $2
$128; no entry is needed
$130; Cash Over and Short is credited $2
$20; Petty Cash is debited
questions.answerText: $130; Cash Over and Short is debited $2
questions.explanation: The fund must be restored to $150, so the check is $150 - $20 = $130. That is $2 more than receipts, which means a shortage.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A shortage is debited to Cash Over and Short.
deepDive.whyCorrect: $130 = $128 expenses + $2 shortage.

wrongReasons.2: The check must cover the missing $2 too.
wrongReasons.3: A credit would mean an overage.
wrongReasons.4: The fund is restored via Cash, not Petty Cash.

questions.stem: The Petty Cash account is debited or credited only when:
options: Any small expense is paid
The fund is replenished
The fund is created or its size changes
Cash is counted
questions.answerText: The fund is created or its size changes
questions.explanation: Normal payments are tracked on receipts. The account balance stays fixed unless the fund size changes.

deepDive.conceptExplain: An imprest fund keeps a fixed total of cash plus receipts.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Only changes to the fund size affect the account.

wrongReasons.1: Expenses are recorded at replenishment.
wrongReasons.2: Replenishment debits expenses and credits Cash.
wrongReasons.4: Counting does not change the account.

questions.stem: A debit balance in Cash Over and Short at year-end means that:
options: The company had net cash shortages
The company had net cash overages
The bank made an error
Cash was recorded twice
questions.answerText: The company had net cash shortages
questions.explanation: Debits increase expenses and losses. Shortages are losses.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Shortages are debited and overages are credited.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A debit balance means shortages exceeded overages.

wrongReasons.2: Overages are credits.
wrongReasons.3: This account is about the company's own cash handling.
wrongReasons.4: Doubles would not be tracked here.

questions.stem: Which task is the best example of independent verification?
options: Someone who does not handle cash prepares the bank reconciliation
The cashier prepares the bank reconciliation
The cashier counts and also deposits the cash alone
A manager signs checks without looking at them
questions.answerText: Someone who does not handle cash prepares the bank reconciliation
questions.explanation: A different person checking the records can catch errors and theft.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Records should be checked by someone not involved in the work.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A person outside the cash function reviews the records.

wrongReasons.2: The cashier would be checking their own work.
wrongReasons.3: No one else is involved.
wrongReasons.4: Signing without review is not a real check.

questions.stem: What is a deposit in transit?
options: A check the company wrote but not yet cashed
A deposit the bank recorded but the company did not
A deposit recorded by the company but not yet shown by the bank
A note collected by the bank
questions.answerText: A deposit recorded by the company but not yet shown by the bank
questions.explanation: It happens when a deposit is made near the end of the month. The bank adds it a day or two later.

deepDive.conceptExplain: These are timing differences, not errors.
deepDive.whyCorrect: The company has recorded it but the bank has not.

wrongReasons.1: That is an outstanding check.
wrongReasons.2: That would be a book-side item.
wrongReasons.4: That is a book-side item.

questions.stem: Which item is usually classified as a cash equivalent?
options: A two-year loan to a supplier
A short-term investment with an original maturity of three months or less
Inventory held for sale
A building
questions.answerText: A short-term investment with an original maturity of three months or less
questions.explanation: Cash equivalents are highly liquid and close to maturity. They can be turned into cash quickly.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Short maturity and low risk are the key features.
deepDive.whyCorrect: An original maturity of three months or less meets the usual test.

wrongReasons.1: Two years is long-term.
wrongReasons.3: Inventory is not cash.
wrongReasons.4: Buildings are long-term assets.

questions.stem: Interest earned on the checking account appears on the bank statement but not in the books. How is it treated on the reconciliation?
options: Subtracted from the bank balance
Added to the bank balance
Added to the book balance
No adjustment
questions.answerText: Added to the book balance
questions.explanation: The bank has increased the account but the company has not. The company adds it on the book side and records Dr Cash / Cr Interest Revenue.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Bank credits missing from the books increase the book balance.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It is a book-side addition.

wrongReasons.1: It has no effect on the bank balance.
wrongReasons.2: The bank balance already includes it.
wrongReasons.4: The books need to be corrected.

questions.stem: What is accounts receivable?
options: Amounts customers owe the company from sales on account
Amounts the company owes suppliers
Cash held at the bank
Written promises to pay interest
questions.answerText: Amounts customers owe the company from sales on account
questions.explanation: Accounts receivable is an asset because the company expects to collect.

deepDive.conceptExplain: It arises from credit sales and is usually collected within the credit terms, often 30 days.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It is what customers owe.

wrongReasons.2: That is accounts payable.
wrongReasons.3: That is cash.
wrongReasons.4: That describes notes.

questions.stem: Why is the allowance method preferred over direct write-off?
options: It is simpler to record
It increases net income
It avoids estimates
It matches bad debt expense with the revenue it helped earn
questions.answerText: It matches bad debt expense with the revenue it helped earn
questions.explanation: The allowance method estimates bad debts in the same period as the related sales. The direct write-off method waits until an account is found uncollectible.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Estimating bad debts follows the matching principle and keeps receivables at a realistic value.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It matches expense to the sales period.

wrongReasons.1: It requires estimates, so it is not simpler.
wrongReasons.2: It tends to lower income in the sale period.
wrongReasons.3: It relies on estimates.

questions.stem: Which entry records the estimate of bad debts under the allowance method?
options: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts / Cr Accounts Receivable
Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Accounts Receivable
Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
Dr Accounts Receivable / Cr Bad Debt Expense
questions.answerText: Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
questions.explanation: The estimate is an adjusting entry. The credit goes to a contra account, not directly to Accounts Receivable.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The allowance is a contra asset account that reduces receivables on the balance sheet.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Expense is debited; the allowance is credited.

wrongReasons.1: That is the write-off entry.
wrongReasons.2: That is the direct write-off method.
wrongReasons.4: That would increase receivables.

questions.stem: Under the allowance method, which entry writes off a specific customer's $400 account?
options: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts 400 / Cr Accounts Receivable 400
Dr Bad Debt Expense 400 / Cr Accounts Receivable 400
Dr Bad Debt Expense 400 / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts 400
Dr Accounts Receivable 400 / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts 400
questions.answerText: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts 400 / Cr Accounts Receivable 400
questions.explanation: The expense was already recorded in the estimate. The write-off just removes the receivable against the allowance.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The write-off does not create a new expense.
deepDive.whyCorrect: The allowance absorbs the loss.

wrongReasons.2: That would double count the expense.
wrongReasons.3: That is the estimate entry.
wrongReasons.4: That would add to the receivable.

questions.stem: Under the allowance method, writing off a specific uncollectible account:
options: Does not change net realizable value
Decreases net income
Increases net realizable value
Decreases net realizable value
questions.answerText: Does not change net realizable value
questions.explanation: Both Accounts Receivable and the allowance fall by the same amount. Their difference stays the same.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Net realizable value = Accounts Receivable - Allowance.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Both parts drop together, so the net stays put.

wrongReasons.2: The expense was already recorded.
wrongReasons.3: Nothing is added.
wrongReasons.4: The net amount does not fall.

questions.stem: Credit sales were $200,000 and the company estimates 1.5% will be uncollectible. What is the bad debt expense?
questions.explanation: Using the percentage-of-sales method, the expense is $200,000 x 1.5% = $3,000.

deepDive.conceptExplain: This method focuses on the income statement. The existing allowance balance is ignored.

wrongReasons.1: That moves the decimal one place too far.
wrongReasons.3: That is 0.75% of sales.
wrongReasons.4: That is 15%.

questions.stem: Accounts Receivable is $60,000 and the company estimates that 5% will not be collected. The allowance has a $800 credit balance before adjusting. What is the bad debt expense?
questions.explanation: The ending allowance should be $60,000 x 5% = $3,000. Since $800 is already there, the expense is $3,000 - $800 = $2,200.

deepDive.conceptExplain: This method sets the ending allowance balance, then adjusts for what is already there.
deepDive.whyCorrect: $3,000 target - $800 existing = $2,200.

wrongReasons.1: That ignores the existing balance.
wrongReasons.2: That adds the balance instead of subtracting it.
wrongReasons.3: That is only the existing balance.

questions.stem: Accounts Receivable is $50,000 and the Allowance for Doubtful Accounts has a $2,500 credit balance. What is net realizable value?
questions.explanation: Subtract the allowance from receivables: $50,000 - $2,500 = $47,500.

deepDive.conceptExplain: This is the amount the company expects to collect.

wrongReasons.2: The allowance is subtracted, not added.
wrongReasons.3: That ignores the allowance.
wrongReasons.4: That is only the allowance.

questions.stem: A customer pays an account that was written off earlier. What is the first step in recording the recovery?
options: Dr Cash / Cr Sales Revenue
Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts / Cr Accounts Receivable
Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Cash
Dr Accounts Receivable / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
questions.answerText: Dr Accounts Receivable / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
questions.explanation: First reverse the write-off, then record the collection (Dr Cash / Cr Accounts Receivable).

deepDive.conceptExplain: The reversal shows that the customer did pay after all.
deepDive.whyCorrect: The write-off is reversed first.

wrongReasons.1: It is not new revenue.
wrongReasons.2: That repeats the write-off.
wrongReasons.3: That makes no sense for a collection.

questions.stem: In the aging method, how is the allowance estimated?
options: By taking a percentage of total cash sales
By multiplying net income by a fixed rate
By writing off the largest accounts
By grouping receivables by how long they have been unpaid
questions.answerText: By grouping receivables by how long they have been unpaid
questions.explanation: Older receivables are less likely to be collected, so they get higher percentages.

deepDive.conceptExplain: An aging schedule applies a different rate to each age group.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It uses how overdue the accounts are.

wrongReasons.1: Cash sales do not create receivables.
wrongReasons.2: Net income is not the base.
wrongReasons.3: Size alone does not decide.

questions.stem: A $6,000 note receivable bears 8% interest for 90 days. Using a 360-day year, how much interest is earned?
questions.explanation: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time = $6,000 x 8% x 90/360 = $120.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Use time as a fraction of a year.

wrongReasons.1: That is a full year's interest.
wrongReasons.2: That is only 30 days' interest.
wrongReasons.4: The result is ten times too large.

questions.stem: A $9,000 note receivable has a 6% rate and a 120-day term (360-day year). What is the maturity value?
questions.explanation: Interest is $9,000 x 6% x 120/360 = $180. Maturity value is principal plus interest, or $9,180.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Maturity value = Principal + Interest.

wrongReasons.1: That is a full year of interest.
wrongReasons.2: That is only 40 days of interest.
wrongReasons.4: That leaves out the interest.

questions.stem: On December 1, the company accepted a $10,000, 9%, 60-day note receivable. What interest should be accrued on December 31?
questions.explanation: One month of interest: $10,000 x 9% x 1/12 = $75. The entry is Dr Interest Receivable 75 / Cr Interest Revenue 75.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Interest earned but not collected is accrued at period end.

wrongReasons.1: That is two months of interest.
wrongReasons.3: That is a full year of interest.
wrongReasons.4: Interest has been earned for one month.

questions.stem: A customer fails to pay a note at maturity. No interest has been accrued yet. What does the company usually record?
options: Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Notes Receivable
Dr Cash / Cr Notes Receivable
No entry
Dr Accounts Receivable for the maturity value / Cr Notes Receivable and Interest Revenue
questions.answerText: Dr Accounts Receivable for the maturity value / Cr Notes Receivable and Interest Revenue
questions.explanation: A dishonored note is moved to Accounts Receivable, including the interest earned. The company still expects to collect.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The debt still exists, so the company keeps the claim.
deepDive.whyCorrect: The note and the interest become a receivable.

wrongReasons.1: Not yet deemed uncollectible.
wrongReasons.2: No cash was received.
wrongReasons.3: The company must still record the change.

questions.stem: What does accounts payable represent?
options: Amounts customers owe the company
Money lent to employees
The company's cash balance
Amounts the company owes suppliers for goods or services bought on account
questions.answerText: Amounts the company owes suppliers for goods or services bought on account
questions.explanation: It is a short-term liability that is usually paid within the credit terms, often 30 days.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Supplier bills not yet paid are accounts payable.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It is what the company owes suppliers.

wrongReasons.1: That is accounts receivable.
wrongReasons.2: That is Advances to Employees.
wrongReasons.3: Cash is an asset.

questions.stem: The company borrows $20,000 by signing a 12-month note with First Valley Bank. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Cash 20,000 / Cr Notes Payable 20,000
Dr Notes Payable 20,000 / Cr Cash 20,000
Dr Cash 20,000 / Cr Notes Receivable 20,000
Dr Cash 20,000 / Cr Interest Payable 20,000
questions.answerText: Dr Cash 20,000 / Cr Notes Payable 20,000
questions.explanation: Cash increases and the company now owes the bank, so Notes Payable increases.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Borrowing creates a liability.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Cash is debited and Notes Payable is credited.

wrongReasons.2: That reverses the entry.
wrongReasons.3: The company is the borrower, not the lender.
wrongReasons.4: No interest has accrued yet.

questions.stem: At year-end, the company has a $12,000, 10% note payable that was issued three months ago. How much interest expense should be accrued?
questions.explanation: $12,000 x 10% x 3/12 = $300. Dr Interest Expense 300 / Cr Interest Payable 300.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Interest builds up over time even if no payment is made.

wrongReasons.2: That is a full year's interest.
wrongReasons.3: That is only one month.
wrongReasons.4: That is 25% of the principal.

questions.stem: What do the terms 2/10, n/30 mean?
options: A 10% discount if paid within 2 days
A 2% penalty after 30 days
A 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days
The full amount is due in 10 days, with a 30% discount
questions.answerText: A 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days
questions.explanation: The buyer can save 2% by paying early. Without the discount, the net amount is due within 30 days.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The first numbers set the discount and discount period; n/30 is the net due date.
deepDive.whyCorrect: 2% for paying in 10 days; net due in 30.

wrongReasons.1: The numbers are reversed.
wrongReasons.2: Terms like these do not impose penalties.
wrongReasons.4: The discount is not 30%.

questions.stem: An invoice for $5,000 has terms 2/10, n/30. The buyer pays on day 8. How much does the buyer pay?
questions.explanation: The discount is $5,000 x 2% = $100, so the payment is $4,900.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The discount applies when payment falls inside the discount period.

wrongReasons.1: Day 8 is within the discount period.
wrongReasons.2: That is a 10% discount.
wrongReasons.3: That treats it as a 0.2% discount.

questions.stem: On December 31, $4,000 of a bank loan is due in six months and the rest is due in three years. How is the $4,000 reported?
options: As a long-term liability
As a current liability
As equity
As an expense
questions.answerText: As a current liability
questions.explanation: The part due within one year is a current liability, even though the loan itself is long-term.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Debt due within one year is classified as current.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Six months is within a year.

wrongReasons.1: That applies only to amounts due after one year.
wrongReasons.3: Loans are not equity.
wrongReasons.4: Principal is not an expense.

questions.stem: The company receives $1,200 for a 12-month service contract before doing any work. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Cash 1,200 / Cr Service Revenue 1,200
Dr Cash 1,200 / Cr Unearned Revenue 1,200
Dr Accounts Receivable 1,200 / Cr Unearned Revenue 1,200
Dr Unearned Revenue 1,200 / Cr Cash 1,200
questions.answerText: Dr Cash 1,200 / Cr Unearned Revenue 1,200
questions.explanation: No service has been performed, so the company owes it. Revenue is recorded later as the work is done.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Cash received in advance is a liability until earned.
deepDive.whyCorrect: The company owes service for the money received.

wrongReasons.1: That recognizes revenue too early.
wrongReasons.3: Cash was received, not owed.
wrongReasons.4: That reverses the entry.

questions.stem: Net credit sales were $360,000 and average accounts receivable was $45,000. What is the receivables turnover ratio?
options: 0.125 times
315 times
45 times
8 times
questions.answerText: 8 times
questions.explanation: Receivables turnover = net credit sales / average receivables = $360,000 / $45,000 = 8.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A higher number means the company collects faster.

wrongReasons.1: That divides the wrong way around.
wrongReasons.2: That subtracts instead of divides.
wrongReasons.3: That is just the average receivables in thousands.

questions.stem: Performed services on account for Maple Supply for $3,000. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Cash 3,000 / Cr Service Revenue 3,000
Dr Accounts Receivable 3,000 / Cr Unearned Revenue 3,000
Dr Service Revenue 3,000 / Cr Accounts Receivable 3,000
Dr Accounts Receivable 3,000 / Cr Service Revenue 3,000
questions.answerText: Dr Accounts Receivable 3,000 / Cr Service Revenue 3,000
questions.explanation: The service was performed, so the revenue is earned. The customer owes the money, so Accounts Receivable is debited.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when earned, even if cash comes later.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A receivable is created and revenue is recognized.

wrongReasons.1: No cash was received.
wrongReasons.2: The work is done, so the revenue is not unearned.
wrongReasons.3: That reverses the entry.

questions.stem: Under the perpetual inventory system, which entries are made when merchandise is sold on account?
options: Debit Accounts Receivable and credit Sales Revenue for the price; debit Cost of Goods Sold and credit Merchandise Inventory for the cost
Debit Accounts Receivable and credit Sales Revenue for the price only; the cost is recorded at year-end
Debit Cost of Goods Sold and credit Sales Revenue; debit Accounts Receivable and credit Merchandise Inventory
Debit Merchandise Inventory and credit Accounts Payable for the cost; debit Cash and credit Sales Revenue for the price
questions.answerText: Debit Accounts Receivable and credit Sales Revenue for the price; debit Cost of Goods Sold and credit Merchandise Inventory for the cost
questions.explanation: A perpetual system records two entries at every sale. One shows the revenue and one moves the cost out of inventory.

deepDive.concept: Perpetual inventory: two entries per sale
deepDive.conceptExplain: With a perpetual system, Merchandise Inventory is updated after every purchase and sale. So each sale needs a revenue entry at the selling price and a cost entry at what the goods cost the company. Together they let you see gross profit on every sale.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It records the revenue at the selling price and then moves the cost from Merchandise Inventory into Cost of Goods Sold.

wrongReasons.2: Waiting until year-end to record cost is the periodic system. A perpetual system records the cost at the time of the sale.
wrongReasons.3: Revenue is credited to Sales Revenue only, and inventory is a credit only when goods leave. This pairing mixes up the accounts and their sides.
wrongReasons.4: This describes buying goods on account and then selling for cash. It does not record the cost of the goods sold.

questions.stem: Goods available for sale were $82,000 ($18,000 of beginning merchandise inventory plus $64,000 of net purchases). Ending merchandise inventory is $21,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold is goods available for sale minus ending inventory. $82,000 - $21,000 = $61,000.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Goods available for sale are beginning inventory plus net purchases. The part still unsold at year-end stays in Merchandise Inventory. Only the rest has been sold and becomes cost of goods sold.

wrongReasons.1: $103,000 adds ending inventory instead of subtracting it.
wrongReasons.3: $82,000 is goods available for sale. You still have to subtract ending inventory.
wrongReasons.4: $21,000 is the ending inventory, the goods that were not sold.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the cost of merchandise inventory?
options: Freight paid to bring purchased goods to the store
The invoice price of the goods, less purchase discounts taken
The cost of delivering sold goods to customers
The invoice price of the goods, less purchase returns
questions.answerText: The cost of delivering sold goods to customers
questions.explanation: Inventory cost includes what it takes to buy the goods and get them to the store. Delivering goods to customers happens after that and is an expense.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Inventory cost is the price paid, adjusted for returns and discounts, plus freight to bring goods to the store. Delivery to customers is Delivery Expense.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Delivery to customers is a selling cost, so it is expensed as Delivery Expense.

wrongReasons.1: Freight-in is part of the cost of getting the goods ready to sell.
wrongReasons.2: Discounts taken lower the cost of the goods, so they are part of inventory cost.
wrongReasons.4: Returns lower the cost of the goods, so they are part of inventory cost.

questions.stem: Purchased merchandise on account for $8,000, terms 2/10, n/30. Merchandise costing $1,500 was returned as defective before payment. The balance was paid within the discount period. How much cash was paid?
questions.explanation: After the return, the invoice is $8,000 - $1,500 = $6,500. The 2% discount applies only to this amount, so the payment is $6,500 x 98% = $6,370.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A purchase return lowers what you owe, so the discount is figured on the remaining balance only. The order matters: subtract returns first, then take the discount on what is left.

wrongReasons.1: $6,500 is the balance after the return but before the 2% discount was taken.
wrongReasons.2: $7,840 takes the discount on the full $8,000 ($8,000 x 98%) and ignores the return.
wrongReasons.3: $6,000 takes off $2,000 in total, but the return was $1,500 and the discount is only 2% of the remaining balance.

questions.stem: Which statement about goods shipped FOB shipping point is correct?
options: The seller owns the goods until they arrive and normally pays the freight
The buyer owns the goods once they are shipped and normally pays the freight
The buyer owns the goods only after payment is made, whoever pays the freight
The carrier owns the goods while they are in transit
questions.answerText: The buyer owns the goods once they are shipped and normally pays the freight
questions.explanation: FOB shipping point means title passes to the buyer at the seller's dock. The buyer is responsible for the goods and the freight from there.

deepDive.conceptExplain: FOB stands for free on board. The point named in the terms is where ownership changes hands. With FOB shipping point, that is when the goods leave the seller, so the buyer carries the risk during shipping.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Title passes when the goods leave the seller, so the buyer owns them in transit and usually pays the freight.

wrongReasons.1: That describes FOB destination, where the seller keeps ownership until arrival.
wrongReasons.3: Ownership does not wait for payment. The FOB terms decide when title passes.
wrongReasons.4: A carrier only delivers the goods. It never takes ownership of them.

questions.stem: At year-end, Bluebird Traders has goods in transit to a customer under FOB destination terms. Who includes these goods in its ending merchandise inventory?
options: Bluebird Traders, the seller
The customer, the buyer
Both companies, so the goods are counted twice
Neither company until the goods are paid for
questions.answerText: Bluebird Traders, the seller
questions.explanation: Under FOB destination, title stays with the seller until the goods reach the buyer. So the seller still counts the goods in its inventory.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Inventory belongs to whoever has title on the balance sheet date. FOB destination keeps title with the seller until delivery. FOB shipping point would put the goods on the buyer's books instead.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Title has not passed yet, so the goods are still the seller's inventory.

wrongReasons.2: The buyer does not get title until the goods arrive under FOB destination.
wrongReasons.3: Goods can never be counted by both parties. That would overstate total inventory.
wrongReasons.4: Payment does not decide ownership. The shipping terms do.

questions.stem: For the year, sales revenue was $90,000, sales returns and allowances were $4,000, sales discounts were $2,000, and cost of goods sold was $52,000. What is gross profit?

deepDive.conceptExplain: Gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold. Net sales are sales revenue less the two contra accounts, Sales Returns and Allowances and Sales Discounts.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Net sales of $84,000 less cost of goods sold of $52,000 equals $32,000.

wrongReasons.1: $38,000 is $90,000 - $52,000. It ignores both contra revenue accounts.
wrongReasons.2: $34,000 deducts the returns but forgets the sales discounts.
wrongReasons.4: $36,000 deducts the discounts but forgets the sales returns and allowances.

questions.stem: Net sales were $200,000 and cost of goods sold was $130,000. What is the gross profit percentage?

deepDive.conceptExplain: The gross profit percentage shows how many cents of each sales dollar are left after paying for the goods. It is gross profit divided by net sales.

wrongReasons.1: 65% is cost of goods sold divided by net sales, not gross profit divided by net sales.
wrongReasons.2: 70% reads the $70,000 gross profit as if it were a percent.
wrongReasons.3: 53.8% divides gross profit by cost of goods sold ($70,000 / $130,000) instead of net sales.

questions.stem: Which statement about Sales Discounts is correct?
options: It is a contra revenue account with a normal debit balance
It is an expense account with a normal debit balance
It is a liability account with a normal credit balance
It is a revenue account with a normal credit balance
questions.answerText: It is a contra revenue account with a normal debit balance
questions.explanation: Sales Discounts reduce Sales Revenue, so it is a contra revenue account. Because revenue is a credit, its contra account has a debit balance.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Sales Discounts and Sales Returns and Allowances are deducted from Sales Revenue to find net sales. They are the opposite of their parent account, so they increase with debits.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It is deducted from Sales Revenue and increases with a debit.

wrongReasons.2: It is not an expense. It sits at the top of the income statement and reduces sales.
wrongReasons.3: No money is owed. A discount given to a customer is not a liability.
wrongReasons.4: A normal credit balance belongs to Sales Revenue itself, not its contra account.

questions.stem: Paid $400 freight on merchandise purchased from Oakridge Supply under FOB shipping point terms. Which entry is correct under the perpetual system?
options: Dr Delivery Expense 400 / Cr Cash 400
Dr Cost of Goods Sold 400 / Cr Cash 400
Dr Cash 400 / Cr Merchandise Inventory 400
Dr Merchandise Inventory 400 / Cr Cash 400
questions.answerText: Dr Merchandise Inventory 400 / Cr Cash 400
questions.explanation: Freight paid to bring goods in is part of the cost of the inventory. So it is debited to Merchandise Inventory.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Any cost needed to get goods ready for sale is added to inventory. Freight paid by the buyer on incoming goods is one of these costs. Freight paid to ship goods out to customers is Delivery Expense.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Freight on incoming goods raises the cost of inventory, so Dr Merchandise Inventory 400 / Cr Cash 400.

wrongReasons.1: Delivery Expense is for shipping goods out to customers, not for goods coming in.
wrongReasons.2: Cost of Goods Sold is only debited when the goods are sold.
wrongReasons.3: This reverses the entry and would lower inventory when cash is paid out.

questions.stem: A customer returned merchandise that had been sold on account for $600 (cost $380). Which entries record the return under the perpetual system?
options: Dr Sales Returns and Allowances 600 / Cr Accounts Receivable 600 only
Dr Sales Revenue 380 / Cr Accounts Receivable 380; Dr Merchandise Inventory 600 / Cr Cost of Goods Sold 600
Dr Sales Returns and Allowances 600 / Cr Accounts Receivable 600; Dr Merchandise Inventory 380 / Cr Cost of Goods Sold 380
Dr Accounts Receivable 600 / Cr Sales Returns and Allowances 600; Dr Cost of Goods Sold 380 / Cr Merchandise Inventory 380
questions.answerText: Dr Sales Returns and Allowances 600 / Cr Accounts Receivable 600; Dr Merchandise Inventory 380 / Cr Cost of Goods Sold 380
questions.explanation: A return reverses the sale at the selling price and reverses the cost at cost. The goods go back into Merchandise Inventory.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A sales return needs two entries under the perpetual system. One lowers revenue and the customer's balance. The other puts the goods back into inventory and lowers cost of goods sold.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Revenue is reversed at $600 and the cost is reversed at $380.

wrongReasons.1: Leaving out the second entry would leave the goods missing from inventory and cost of goods sold too high.
wrongReasons.2: The amounts are swapped. Revenue is reversed at the selling price and inventory returns at cost.
wrongReasons.4: The sides are backwards. A return lowers Accounts Receivable, so it must be credited.

questions.stem: Merchandise inventory: 100 units at $10 were on hand, then 200 units at $12 were bought. 150 units were sold. Using FIFO, what is the cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: FIFO sells the oldest units first: 100 units at $10 is $1,000, plus 50 units at $12 is $600. The total is $1,600.

deepDive.conceptExplain: First-in, first-out assumes the oldest costs leave inventory first. So cost of goods sold uses the earliest prices and ending inventory holds the latest prices.

wrongReasons.1: $1,800 is 150 units at $12. That is the LIFO answer.
wrongReasons.3: $1,700 is the weighted-average answer, 150 units at about $11.33.
wrongReasons.4: $2,200 uses 100 units at $10 and 100 units at $12, which is 200 units. Only 150 units were sold.

questions.stem: Merchandise inventory: 100 units at $10 were on hand, then 200 units at $12 were bought. 150 units were sold. Using LIFO, what is the cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: LIFO sells the newest units first, so all 150 units come from the $12 purchase. The cost is 150 x $12 = $1,800.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Last-in, first-out assumes the most recent costs leave inventory first. When prices rise, LIFO gives a higher cost of goods sold than FIFO.

wrongReasons.1: $1,600 is the FIFO answer, using the oldest $10 units first.
wrongReasons.2: $1,700 is the weighted-average answer.
wrongReasons.4: $1,500 is 150 units at the oldest price of $10 and ignores the newer purchase.

questions.stem: The company had 200 units at $6 and bought 100 more units at $9. It sold 240 units. Using the weighted-average method, what is the cost of the 60 units left in ending inventory?
questions.explanation: Total cost is 200 x $6 + 100 x $9 = $2,100 for 300 units, an average of $7. Ending inventory is 60 x $7 = $420.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Weighted average divides total cost of goods available by total units to get one average cost per unit. Both cost of goods sold and ending inventory use that same average.

wrongReasons.1: $360 is 60 units at the older $6 price, which is not the average.
wrongReasons.2: $540 is 60 units at the newest $9 price, which is not the average.
wrongReasons.3: $450 uses a simple average of the two prices ($7.50), which ignores how many units were bought at each price.

questions.stem: When purchase prices are rising, which statement comparing FIFO and LIFO is correct?
options: FIFO reports a higher gross profit than LIFO
FIFO reports a lower ending inventory than LIFO
LIFO reports a higher gross profit than FIFO
FIFO and LIFO report the same gross profit
questions.answerText: FIFO reports a higher gross profit than LIFO
questions.explanation: With rising prices, FIFO charges the older, lower costs to cost of goods sold. That leaves a higher gross profit than LIFO.

deepDive.concept: FIFO vs LIFO when prices rise
deepDive.conceptExplain: The method changes which costs go to expense and which stay in inventory. Rising prices make FIFO's cost of goods sold lower and its ending inventory higher than LIFO's.
deepDive.whyCorrect: FIFO's lower cost of goods sold means a higher gross profit.

wrongReasons.2: FIFO's ending inventory holds the newest, higher costs, so it is higher, not lower.
wrongReasons.3: LIFO charges the newest, higher costs to expense, so its gross profit is lower.
wrongReasons.4: Different cost flow assumptions give different numbers when prices change.

questions.stem: Which cost flow method values ending merchandise inventory closest to current replacement cost when prices are rising?
options: LIFO
FIFO
Weighted average
None of the three methods affects inventory value
questions.answerText: FIFO
questions.explanation: FIFO leaves the most recent purchases in ending inventory. Those costs are closest to today's prices.

deepDive.concept: Inventory valuation on the balance sheet
deepDive.conceptExplain: Ending inventory under FIFO is made up of the latest purchases. LIFO leaves the oldest costs on the balance sheet, which can look out of date after years of rising prices.
deepDive.whyCorrect: FIFO's ending inventory consists of the newest costs.

wrongReasons.1: LIFO leaves the oldest costs in inventory, which are the furthest from current prices.
wrongReasons.3: Weighted average blends old and new costs, so it falls between the two.
wrongReasons.4: The method chosen changes the ending inventory number.

questions.stem: Sold merchandise on account to Redwood Studio for $3,000, terms 2/10, n/30. Redwood Studio paid within the discount period. How much cash did the company receive?
questions.explanation: The discount is 2% of $3,000, or $60. Cash received is $3,000 - $60 = $2,940.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The seller records the discount in Sales Discounts, a contra revenue account. The entry is Dr Cash 2,940, Dr Sales Discounts 60, Cr Accounts Receivable 3,000.

wrongReasons.1: $3,000 would only be received if the customer paid after the discount period.
wrongReasons.3: $2,700 takes 10% off. The 10 in 2/10 is the number of days.
wrongReasons.4: $3,060 adds the discount instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Cost of Goods Sold?
options: The cost of all merchandise purchased during the period
The selling price of the merchandise sold to customers
The cost of merchandise still on hand at the end of the period
The cost of the merchandise that was sold to customers during the period
questions.answerText: The cost of the merchandise that was sold to customers during the period
questions.explanation: Cost of Goods Sold is an expense that shows what the company paid for the goods it actually sold. Goods still on hand stay in Merchandise Inventory.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Merchandise Inventory is an asset until the goods are sold. When they are sold, their cost moves to the expense account Cost of Goods Sold and is matched with the sales revenue.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It matches the cost of goods sold with the revenue they earned.

wrongReasons.1: Purchases not yet sold are still inventory, which is an asset.
wrongReasons.2: The selling price is revenue, not cost.
wrongReasons.3: Goods on hand at period-end are Merchandise Inventory.

questions.stem: Merchandise Inventory began at $9,000. During the year the company purchased merchandise for $30,000, returned $2,000 of it, and paid $1,500 freight-in. Cost of Goods Sold recorded for the year was $28,000. What is the ending balance of Merchandise Inventory?
questions.explanation: Start with $9,000, add $30,000 and $1,500, then subtract the $2,000 return and the $28,000 cost of goods sold. The ending balance is $10,500.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Under the perpetual system the Merchandise Inventory account is a running balance. Purchases and freight-in increase it. Returns and cost of goods sold decrease it.

wrongReasons.2: $9,000 ignores all activity during the year.
wrongReasons.3: $12,500 forgets to subtract the $2,000 purchase return.
wrongReasons.4: $8,500 subtracts the freight-in instead of adding it.

questions.stem: Under terms 2/10, n/30, how much must a buyer pay on Day 20 for a $12,000 invoice dated Day 1?
options: $11,760, because the discount still applies
$11,880, because half the discount applies
$12,000, because the discount period has passed
$12,240, because a late fee is added
questions.answerText: $12,000, because the discount period has passed
questions.explanation: The 10-day discount period ended on Day 10. Paying on Day 20 means paying the full invoice, which is still due by Day 30.

deepDive.conceptExplain: In 2/10, n/30 the first number is the discount percent and the second is the discount period in days. After day 10 the discount is gone, and the full amount is due on day 30.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Day 20 is after the 10-day window, so the full $12,000 is due.

wrongReasons.1: The 2% discount ended on Day 10, so $11,760 is no longer allowed.
wrongReasons.2: These terms do not offer partial discounts.
wrongReasons.4: These terms say nothing about late fees. The invoice amount stays $12,000 until Day 30.

questions.stem: The perpetual inventory records show $42,000, but a physical count shows $40,500. Which adjusting entry records the shrinkage?
options: Dr Merchandise Inventory 1,500 / Cr Cost of Goods Sold 1,500
Dr Loss from Theft 42,000 / Cr Merchandise Inventory 42,000
Dr Cost of Goods Sold 40,500 / Cr Merchandise Inventory 40,500
Dr Cost of Goods Sold 1,500 / Cr Merchandise Inventory 1,500
questions.answerText: Dr Cost of Goods Sold 1,500 / Cr Merchandise Inventory 1,500
questions.explanation: Shrinkage means less inventory exists than the records show. The $1,500 difference is written off to Cost of Goods Sold.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A physical count can reveal lost, damaged, or stolen goods. The adjusting entry lowers Merchandise Inventory to the counted amount and normally charges the difference to Cost of Goods Sold.
deepDive.whyCorrect: $42,000 - $40,500 = $1,500 is expensed and removed from inventory.

wrongReasons.1: This entry would increase inventory, but the count shows a shortage.
wrongReasons.2: Only the $1,500 difference is lost, not the entire $42,000.
wrongReasons.3: The adjustment is the shortage of $1,500, not the counted balance of $40,500.

questions.stem: Which statement about Sales Returns and Allowances is correct?
options: It is an expense account that is added to Cost of Goods Sold
It is a contra revenue account that is deducted from Sales Revenue
It is an asset account that is added to Accounts Receivable
It is a liability account owed to customers
questions.answerText: It is a contra revenue account that is deducted from Sales Revenue
questions.explanation: Returns and allowances lower the revenue earned from sales. They are tracked in a contra revenue account with a debit balance.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Keeping returns in a separate account lets managers see how much merchandise comes back. At year-end the balance is deducted from Sales Revenue when finding net sales.
deepDive.whyCorrect: It reduces sales and is shown as a deduction on the income statement.

wrongReasons.1: Returns are not an expense and do not belong in Cost of Goods Sold.
wrongReasons.3: It lowers receivables when recorded, so it is not an asset to add.
wrongReasons.4: A return on account reduces what the customer owes. It does not create a liability.

questions.stem: Which cost should be debited to the Equipment account when a company buys a new machine?
options: The first year's insurance premium on the machine
Routine oil changes after the machine is in use
Freight paid to deliver the machine to the company
Training for employees on how to use the machine
questions.answerText: Freight paid to deliver the machine to the company
questions.explanation: Costs needed to get an asset to its location and ready for use are capitalized. Freight on delivery qualifies.

deepDive.conceptExplain: The cost of a plant asset includes its purchase price plus all reasonable costs to bring it to the place and condition for use, such as freight and installation. Ongoing costs and training are expenses.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Delivery freight is a cost of getting the machine ready for use, so it is added to Equipment.

wrongReasons.1: Insurance covers a future period, so it is Prepaid Insurance and then Insurance Expense.
wrongReasons.2: Routine maintenance is Repairs and Maintenance Expense.
wrongReasons.4: Training is an expense and does not add to the machine's cost.

questions.stem: Equipment costing $48,000 has a salvage value of $6,000 and a useful life of 7 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
questions.explanation: Depreciable cost is $48,000 - $6,000 = $42,000. Divided by 7 years, annual depreciation is $6,000.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Straight-line spreads the depreciable cost evenly over the useful life. Depreciable cost is cost minus salvage value.

wrongReasons.2: $6,857 divides the full cost by 7 and forgets to subtract salvage value.
wrongReasons.3: $7,000 divides the depreciable cost by 6 years instead of 7.
wrongReasons.4: $5,250 comes from dividing $42,000 by 8 years, a life the question did not give.

questions.stem: Purchased equipment on October 1 for $30,000. Salvage value is $3,000 and the useful life is 5 years (straight-line). The year ends December 31. What is the depreciation expense for the first year?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation is ($30,000 - $3,000) / 5 = $5,400. The equipment was used for 3 of 12 months, so $5,400 x 3/12 = $1,350.

deepDive.conceptExplain: When an asset is bought during the year, depreciation is prorated by the number of months it was in use. Start with a full year's amount, then multiply by the months over 12.

wrongReasons.1: $5,400 is a full year of depreciation, but the asset was used only 3 months.
wrongReasons.3: $1,500 prorates correctly but forgets to subtract salvage value ($30,000 / 5 x 3/12).
wrongReasons.4: $4,050 prorates for 9 months, which is the part of the year before the purchase.

questions.stem: Equipment cost $40,000, salvage value is $4,000, and useful life is 5 years. Using double-declining-balance, what is the first-year depreciation expense?
questions.explanation: The straight-line rate is 20%, so the double rate is 40%. Salvage is not subtracted from the base: $40,000 x 40% = $16,000.

deepDive.conceptExplain: DDB uses twice the straight-line rate and applies it to the book value at the start of each year. Salvage value is not subtracted from the base, but book value may never go below salvage.

wrongReasons.2: $7,200 is the straight-line amount ($36,000 / 5).
wrongReasons.3: $14,400 subtracts salvage first ($36,000 x 40%), which DDB does not do.
wrongReasons.4: $8,000 uses only the 20% straight-line rate on the cost.

questions.stem: Using the same equipment (cost $40,000, salvage $4,000, 5-year life, double-declining-balance), what is the second-year depreciation expense?
questions.explanation: After year 1 the book value is $40,000 - $16,000 = $24,000. Year 2 depreciation is $24,000 x 40% = $9,600.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Each year's DDB expense is the rate times the book value at the start of that year. Book value falls each year, so the expense falls too. Book value may never go below salvage value.

wrongReasons.1: $16,000 repeats the first year's amount. The base must be reduced by year 1 depreciation.
wrongReasons.2: $14,400 applies 40% to the cost less salvage, which is the wrong base.
wrongReasons.4: $6,400 applies 40% to a book value of $16,000, which was the year 1 expense and not the book value.

questions.stem: A delivery truck cost $90,000 and has a salvage value of $9,000. It is expected to be driven 270,000 miles. The truck was driven 20,000 miles this year. Using units-of-activity, what is depreciation expense?
questions.explanation: The rate per mile is ($90,000 - $9,000) / 270,000 = $0.30. For 20,000 miles, depreciation is $6,000.

deepDive.conceptExplain: This method links depreciation to use. Find the cost per unit by dividing depreciable cost by total expected units, then multiply by the units used.

wrongReasons.1: $6,667 divides the full $90,000 by 270,000 miles ($0.333 per mile) and forgets to subtract salvage value.
wrongReasons.2: $7,500 would need a rate of $0.375 per mile, which does not come from the data.
wrongReasons.3: $5,400 would need a rate of $0.27 per mile, which does not come from the data.

questions.stem: Equipment with a cost of $20,000 and accumulated depreciation of $14,000 is sold for exactly its book value. What is the result?
options: A gain of $6,000
No gain or loss is recorded
A loss of $6,000
A gain of $14,000
questions.answerText: No gain or loss is recorded
questions.explanation: Book value is $20,000 - $14,000 = $6,000. When the sale price equals book value, there is no gain or loss.

deepDive.conceptExplain: A gain or loss on disposal is the difference between the cash received and the asset's book value. If they are the same, the difference is zero.
deepDive.whyCorrect: The $6,000 received equals the $6,000 book value, so there is nothing to record as a gain or loss.

wrongReasons.1: A $6,000 gain would mean the equipment was sold for $12,000.
wrongReasons.3: A $6,000 loss would mean the equipment was sold for nothing.
wrongReasons.4: $14,000 is accumulated depreciation, which is not the same as a gain.

questions.stem: Equipment cost $25,000 with accumulated depreciation of $18,500 was sold for $7,500 cash. What gain or loss resulted from the sale?
options: Loss of $1,000
Gain of $7,500
Gain of $6,500
Gain of $1,000
questions.answerText: Gain of $1,000
questions.explanation: Book value is $25,000 - $18,500 = $6,500. The company received $7,500, which is $1,000 more than book value, so it is a gain.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Compare cash received with book value. If cash is higher, record a gain, which is a credit to Gain on Sale of Equipment. If it is lower, record a loss.

wrongReasons.1: A loss would mean the cash received was lower than book value.
wrongReasons.2: $7,500 is the cash received, not the gain.
wrongReasons.3: $6,500 is the book value, not the gain.

questions.stem: Equipment cost $20,000 with accumulated depreciation of $14,000 was sold for $4,500 cash. What was the gain or loss?
options: Gain of $1,500
Loss of $4,500
Loss of $1,500
Gain of $4,500
questions.answerText: Loss of $1,500
questions.explanation: Book value is $20,000 - $14,000 = $6,000. The cash received of $4,500 is $1,500 less than book value, so there is a loss.

deepDive.conceptExplain: When an asset is sold for less than its book value, the shortfall is a loss. It is recorded as Loss on Sale of Equipment, a debit.

wrongReasons.1: Selling below book value cannot produce a gain.
wrongReasons.2: $4,500 is the cash received, not the loss.
wrongReasons.4: A gain would need the sale price to be above book value.

questions.stem: Sold equipment for more than its book value. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Cash, Dr Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment / Cr Equipment, Cr Gain on Sale of Equipment
Dr Cash, Dr Gain on Sale of Equipment / Cr Equipment, Cr Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment
Dr Cash, Dr Equipment / Cr Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment, Cr Gain on Sale of Equipment
Dr Cash, Dr Loss on Sale of Equipment / Cr Equipment, Cr Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment
questions.answerText: Dr Cash, Dr Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment / Cr Equipment, Cr Gain on Sale of Equipment
questions.explanation: The equipment and its accumulated depreciation are both removed. The extra cash is a gain, which is credited.

deepDive.conceptExplain: To dispose of equipment, debit Cash for the amount received, debit Accumulated Depreciation to remove it, and credit Equipment for its cost. The balancing amount is a credit gain or a debit loss.
deepDive.whyCorrect: A gain is a credit, and the asset and its accumulated depreciation are taken off the books.

wrongReasons.2: A gain must be credited, and accumulated depreciation must be debited to remove it.
wrongReasons.3: Equipment is credited to remove it, and accumulated depreciation is debited.
wrongReasons.4: This records a loss, but the sale produced a gain.

questions.stem: Which statement about depreciation is correct?
options: It measures the current market value of the asset
It allocates the cost of a plant asset to expense over its useful life
It sets aside cash to replace the asset
It is recorded only when the asset is sold
questions.answerText: It allocates the cost of a plant asset to expense over its useful life
questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset across the years that benefit from it. It is an allocation of cost, not a valuation.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Depreciation follows the matching principle. The cost of a long-lived asset is an expense in the periods in which the asset helps earn revenue.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Depreciation matches the asset's cost with the periods it is used.

wrongReasons.1: Book value rarely equals market value, because depreciation follows a cost schedule.
wrongReasons.3: Depreciation is a non-cash expense. It does not put money aside.
wrongReasons.4: Depreciation is recorded each period, not just at the sale.

questions.stem: Which statement about land is correct?
options: Land is depreciated over 20 years
Land is depreciated using the units-of-activity method
Land is not depreciated because it does not wear out
Land is depreciated like a building but with a higher rate
questions.answerText: Land is not depreciated because it does not wear out
questions.explanation: Land is considered to have an unlimited useful life. So no depreciation expense is recorded for it.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Depreciation applies to assets whose usefulness is used up over time, such as buildings, equipment, vehicles, and furniture. Land has an indefinite life, so it stays at cost. Land improvements, such as parking lots, are depreciated.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Land has an unlimited life, so it is not depreciated.

wrongReasons.1: No fixed 20-year life is assumed for land.
wrongReasons.2: Units-of-activity is a method for assets that wear out. Land does not.
wrongReasons.4: Land is not depreciated at any rate.

questions.stem: Compare straight-line and double-declining-balance methods for the same asset. Which is correct?
options: Straight-line gives more expense in the early years than double-declining-balance
Double-declining-balance gives the same expense every year
The two methods give different total depreciation over the life of the asset
Straight-line gives the same expense every year, while double-declining-balance gives more expense in the early years
questions.answerText: Straight-line gives the same expense every year, while double-declining-balance gives more expense in the early years
questions.explanation: DDB front-loads expense because it applies a high rate to a large book value. Straight-line charges equal amounts each year.

deepDive.conceptExplain: Both methods end with the same total depreciation over the asset's life (cost minus salvage). They differ only in how the expense is spread across the years.
deepDive.whyCorrect: Straight-line is level, while DDB is higher at first and lower later.

wrongReasons.1: It is the other way around. DDB has more expense early.
wrongReasons.2: DDB expense falls each year because book value falls.
